opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most underrated shifts happening right now. When we talk about agents, people usually focus on the model side: can it plan, can it use tools, can it run for hours without going off the rails. But once an agent is actually doing real work for you, the human's role quietly changes. You're no longer the person doing the task. You become the person judging whether the task was done well.

That sounds simple, but it's actually very hard. In a chat setting, evaluation is cheap: you read one answer and you know whether you like it. With an agent, the output might be a whole codebase, a research report, or a sequence of fifty actions. You often can't verify every step. So the human becomes something like a reviewer or a manager, and the quality of the whole system starts to depend heavily on how good that person's judgment is.

There are a few layers to this. First, people define what "good" means. The agent can optimize, but it needs a target, and much of that target is tacit. It lives in your taste and your context, things you never wrote down. Second, people catch the failures that are hard to spot automatically: the result that looks plausible but is subtly wrong, or technically correct but useless. Third, and this matters most for model builders, every time a person accepts, rejects, or edits what an agent did, that's a signal. At scale, those signals become one of the most valuable sources of feedback for improving the models. In a sense, users are collectively shaping the reward.

There's also a risk. As agents get more capable, the gap between what they produce and what a person can easily check keeps growing. If people get lazy, or simply can't keep up, you end up rubber-stamping outputs, and the feedback loop degrades. So I think a key question for the next few years is how to design agents that make themselves evaluable. They should show their reasoning, surface uncertainty, and break work into pieces a person can actually check. That way the human stays a meaningful judge rather than just a formality.

So my view is that the human's role doesn't disappear as agents get stronger. It moves up a level. Execution gets delegated, but judgment, taste, and responsibility stay with people, and those become even more important.

r001.rationale: The response says people catch failures in agent outputs and that accepting, rejecting, or editing an agent’s work provides feedback, identifying how people point out mistakes as evaluators.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most important thing to realize is that when you interact with an agent, you stop being a user in the traditional sense and you become something closer to a manager. With a chatbot, the loop is tight: you ask, it answers, you judge immediately whether the answer is good. With an agent, you hand over a task, it goes away for ten minutes or an hour, it takes dozens of actions, and then it comes back and says "done." And the question becomes: how do you know?

So the evaluator role is really about verification under asymmetry. The agent has seen far more of the process than you have. It read the files, ran the commands, made the intermediate decisions. You only see the summary. That means the burden shifts to the person to decide what to check, and that's actually a skill. A good evaluator doesn't re-read everything, because then there was no point delegating. Instead they learn where the agent tends to be unreliable and probe exactly those spots. Did it actually run the tests, or did it say it ran the tests? Did it finish the whole scope, or did it quietly do the easy eighty percent?

The second thing I'd say is that people are evaluators whether they intend to be or not. Every acceptance, every correction, every "no, not like that" is a signal. In the research lab that signal is literal training data. But even in daily use, the way you respond shapes what the agent does next in that session, and increasingly across sessions through memory. So you're not just grading the output, you're shaping the behavior. And people underestimate how much their own sloppiness as an evaluator gets reflected back at them. If you accept vague reports, you train yourself and the system to tolerate vagueness.

The third thing is that the evaluator's job is getting harder, not easier, as models improve. When the agent was obviously weak, errors were obvious. Now the errors are subtle: a plausible-looking result that's wrong in one detail, a confident claim that was never verified. So the human has to move up a level. You can't compete with the agent on execution, but you can own the definition of what "correct" means, what matters, what the constraints are. That's the part the agent can't fully supply from inside the task.

So my short answer would be: the person is the one who holds the standard. The agent proposes, the person decides whether the standard was met, and the quality of that judgment ends up being the ceiling on the whole system.

r001.rationale: The response says that corrections such as “no, not like that” are evaluator signals, and describes checking where the agent may be unreliable. This clearly presents pointing out mistakes as part of evaluating an agent.

astra-6.text:
I think people play two roles at once: they’re users, but they’re also evaluators. When you interact with an AI agent, you’re not just asking whether its answer is correct. You’re judging whether it understood your intention, whether its actions were appropriate, and whether the result actually helped you.

With an agent, that judgment extends to the process. Did it ask for clarification when it needed to? Did it make a reasonable decision on its own? Did it give you enough visibility to intervene? A good final result matters, but so does how the agent gets there.

The challenge is that people don’t always have a clear evaluation standard in advance. Sometimes we discover what we want only after seeing what the agent does. So evaluation becomes an ongoing conversation: the agent acts, we respond, and through that interaction we make our expectations clearer. That makes human feedback valuable, but it also means we shouldn’t treat every individual reaction as an objective measure of quality.

r001.rationale: The response describes judging the agent and giving ongoing feedback, but does not clearly identify pointing out its mistakes as an evaluator action.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people play two roles. They’re users trying to get something done, and they’re evaluators deciding whether the agent has actually helped. Those judgments are related, but they’re not always the same. An answer can sound convincing and still fail to solve the problem.

So the important thing is to make the goal and the criteria clear. Did the agent understand my intention? Did it take appropriate actions? Is the result correct, and how much effort did I have to spend correcting it? With an agent, we need to evaluate the process as well as the final answer.

At the same time, human feedback isn’t a perfect signal. People have different preferences, and they may not have the expertise to recognize every mistake. I see evaluation as a collaboration: people provide context, judgment, and boundaries, while the agent makes its work easy to inspect and correct. Ultimately, the question is whether it helps people achieve what they actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response discusses judging correctness and the effort needed to correct an agent, but does not clearly identify pointing out the agent’s mistakes during interaction as a way people act as evaluators.
